title: Evaluating AI Search: A Practical Framework for Augmented AI Systems — Quotient AI + Tavily

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's primary focus is evaluation methodology for AI search systems, comparing static vs dynamic benchmarks, analyzing LLM judge limitations, and proposing reference-free metrics. The systems being evaluated are RAG and SAG search infrastructure, placing the work in the search and knowledge domain. The talk centers on evaluation methodology with additional context on production monitoring of live AI search agents. Requires prerequisite familiarity with RAG, retrieval evaluation concepts, and LLM-as-judge approaches. A conference presentation recorded at the AI Engineer World's Fair with live demos and experimental results. summary: The presentation covers evaluating AI search systems, a collaboration between Quotient AI (observability for AI apps) and Tavily (web infrastructure for AI agents). Julia frames the core challenge: traditional monitoring can't handle dynamic AI agents that make real-time decisions in changing environments with interconnected failure modes. Quotient's approach uses expert evaluators to detect failures without ground truth data. Tavily's Maitar explains their infrastructure provides real-time web data for language models, with use cases from legal assistants to fraud detection. Two evaluation principles guide their work: the web changes constantly so evaluation must keep pace, and truth is often subjective and contextual. They compare static datasets (SimpleQA, HotpotQA) against dynamic datasets generated by Tavily's open-source LangGraph-based agent, which creates domain-specific queries, aggregates grounding documents from multiple search providers to minimize bias, generates evidence-based Q&A pairs, and tracks experiments via LangSmith. Deanna presents a two-part experiment evaluating six anonymized AI search providers. Dynamic benchmark scores were substantially lower than static scores and relative provider rankings changed considerably—one provider ranked worst on SimpleQA but best on the dynamic benchmark. The LLM judge was imperfect, sometimes flagging correct answers as incorrect and missing hallucinations in surrounding text. The talk then introduces three reference-free metrics: answer completeness (fully addressed, unaddressed, or unknown), document relevance (percent of retrieved documents relevant to the question), and hallucination detection (facts not supported by retrieved documents). Answer completeness rankings correlated 0.94 with dynamic benchmark performance. Only three of six providers returned retrieved documents, with the majority providing only citations—limiting transparency and debugging. Document relevance showed strong inverse correlation with unknown answers. Surprisingly, hallucination rate correlated directly with document relevance: Provider X had the highest hallucination rate yet also highest document relevance, completeness, and correctness, suggesting detailed, thorough responses create more hallucination opportunities. The speakers emphasize metric trade-offs: excelling in one dimension may come at the expense of another. Combined metrics enable diagnostic debugging—for example, incomplete responses with relevant documents and no hallucinations suggest retrieving more documents. The talk concludes with a vision of self-improving AI systems that detect outdated information, unreliable sources, and hallucinations mid-conversation without human intervention.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

Static benchmarks like SimpleQA and HotpotQA are insufficient for evaluating real-time AI search because ground truth is a moving target and truth is often subjective
Dynamic evaluation sets are essential for benchmarking RAG systems in production: they provide real-world alignment, broad coverage, and continuous relevancy

sections.title: Introduction and Fundamental Challenge
sections.summary: Julia introduces the three speakers and frames the core problem: traditional monitoring can't keep up with dynamic AI agents that operate in changing environments with multiple interconnected failure modes. Quotient monitors live AI agents with expert evaluators without waiting for ground truth. The collaboration began when Tavily's founder posed the challenge of building production-ready AI search agents facing web unpredictability and user unpredictability.

sections.title: Tavily Context and Evaluation Principles
sections.summary: Maitar explains Tavily builds infrastructure for agent interaction at scale, providing real-time web data to language models. Use cases include legal assistants, sports news agents, and fraud detection. Two evaluation principles: the web changes constantly so evaluation must keep pace, and truth is often subjective and contextual, requiring unbiased and fair methods.

sections.title: Static vs Dynamic Datasets and Tavily's Open-Source Agent
sections.summary: Discusses SimpleQA and HotpotQA as static benchmarks with limitations for real-time systems. Introduces Tavily's open-source LangGraph-based agent for generating dynamic eval sets: generates domain-specific queries, aggregates documents from multiple search providers to minimize bias, generates evidence-based Q&A pairs, and tracks via LangSmith. Future work includes multi-hop questions, fairness/coverage, and a supervisor node.

sections.title: Two-Part Evaluation Experiment and Static vs Dynamic Results
sections.summary: Deanna presents a two-part evaluation of six anonymized AI search providers comparing static (SimpleQA) vs dynamic (~1000 rows) benchmarks using the SimpleQA correctness LLM judge. Dynamic scores were substantially lower and provider rankings changed considerably. Shows LLM judge limitations: misclassifying correct answers and missing hallucinations. Transitions to reference-free metrics as an alternative, introducing Quotient's answer completeness metric.

sections.title: Reference-Free Metrics Results and Diagnostic Framework
sections.summary: Deanna presents results for three reference-free metrics. Answer completeness (fully addressed/unaddressed/unknown) correlated 0.94 with dynamic benchmark rankings. Only three of six providers returned retrieved documents; the rest provided only citations, limiting transparency. Document relevance showed strong inverse correlation with unknown answers. Hallucination rate correlated directly with document relevance—Provider X had highest hallucination but also highest completeness and correctness, suggesting thorough responses create more hallucination opportunities. Combined metrics enable diagnostic debugging (e.g., incomplete response with relevant docs and no hallucinations suggests retrieving more documents). Julia concludes with a vision of self-improving AI systems that detect outdated information and hallucinations mid-conversation without human intervention.
